title: Clover — 4yo Lop rabbit: acute head tilt and rolling
presentation: 4-year-old male neutered Lop rabbit, sudden onset of a left head tilt yesterday evening, now rolling when startled. Housed indoors with one other rabbit, eating a little hay this morning.

stages.title: Localise the lesion
stages.briefing: Left head tilt of about 40°, horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase to the right, ataxia with rolling to the left. No facial paresis, palpebral reflex intact. Menace present bilaterally. Both ears: clean canals, no discharge, tympanic membranes intact on otoscopy. Temperature 38.9°C. Caecotrophs present, teeth grossly normal on conscious examination.
stages.prompt: Which findings help you localise this vestibular disease?

options.label: Horizontal nystagmus with a constant fast phase
options.detail: Typical of peripheral vestibular disease

options.label: Head tilt with no facial nerve deficit
options.detail: Argues against middle-ear disease tracking to the facial nerve

options.label: Normal menace and no proprioceptive deficits
options.detail: No evidence of a central lesion yet

options.label: Clean external ear canals
options.detail: A normal canal says nothing about the middle ear

options.label: Caecotrophs present
options.detail: Reassuring about gut function, irrelevant to the localisation

stages.explanation: A constant horizontal nystagmus with normal mentation and no proprioceptive deficit points peripheral; a vertical or positional nystagmus, or a rabbit that cannot walk a straight line for reasons other than the tilt, would push you central. Clean canals are the trap: otitis media sits behind an intact tympanum and is invisible on otoscopy.

stages.title: Build the work-up
stages.briefing: The owner will fund a proportionate work-up today and wants to know what each test will tell them.

options.label: Encephalitozoon cuniculi serology — IgG and IgM
options.detail: Paired titres separate exposure from active disease

options.label: Skull radiographs or CT of the tympanic bullae
options.detail: The only way to see middle-ear disease

options.label: Haematology and biochemistry with urea and creatinine
options.detail: E. cuniculi damages kidney as well as brain

options.label: Urinalysis
options.detail: Renal involvement, and it is cheap

options.label: Otoscopy under sedation with a myringotomy if the bulla looks involved
options.detail: Cytology and culture of what is actually in there

options.label: Faecal parasitology
options.detail: Coccidia do not cause a head tilt

options.label: MRI as the first-line test
options.detail: Best imaging, but it does not change today and the bullae come first

stages.explanation: Two diagnoses account for most rabbit head tilts — E. cuniculi and otitis media, usually Pasteurella — and they are distinguished by serology plus imaging of the bullae, not by clinical signs. IgM matters: IgG alone tells you a rabbit met the parasite, which most have. The renal panel is not padding, because the same organism scars kidneys.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: E. cuniculi IgG strongly positive, IgM positive. CT: both tympanic bullae air-filled and normally shaped, no soft tissue, no bone lysis. Urea 9.1 mmol/L (ref 3.6–8.9), creatinine 168 µmol/L (ref 44–150), USG 1.012. Haematology: mild lymphocytosis, no neutrophilia. Blood glucose 7.9 mmol/L.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Active encephalitozoonosis, not just past exposure
options.detail: A positive IgM alongside IgG

options.label: Renal involvement by the same organism
options.detail: Mild azotaemia with poorly concentrated urine

options.label: Otitis media is excluded as the cause
options.detail: Normal, air-filled bullae on CT

options.label: Bacterial otitis interna is still likely
options.detail: Contradicted by the imaging and the normal white cell count

options.label: A cerebrovascular accident is now the leading diagnosis
options.detail: Possible in theory, but nothing here supports it over a confirmed infection

stages.explanation: IgM is what turns a serological curiosity into a diagnosis: most pet rabbits carry IgG, so a positive IgG alone would have left you where you started. Air-filled bullae on CT take otitis media off the list, which is exactly what the imaging was for. The azotaemia with dilute urine is the second organ the parasite has reached, and it changes the drug doses you choose.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: IgM and IgG positive, bullae normal on CT, mild azotaemia with USG 1.012, peripheral vestibular signs.

options.label: Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection with vestibular and renal involvement
options.detail: Active infection, two organs affected

options.label: Otitis media with secondary otitis interna
options.detail: Excluded by normal bullae on CT

options.label: Past E. cuniculi exposure with an unrelated head tilt
options.detail: IgM positivity says the infection is active

options.label: Cerebral toxoplasmosis
options.detail: Rare in rabbits and unsupported by any result here

options.label: Chronic kidney disease with uraemic encephalopathy
options.detail: The azotaemia is far too mild to explain these signs

stages.explanation: Naming the renal involvement in the diagnosis is what stops it being forgotten: fenbendazole for the parasite, but every subsequent NSAID and fluid decision is made for a rabbit with damaged kidneys. Prognosis follows the same logic — vestibular signs often improve, the nephropathy does not.
